Making the classroom available

A few things I'm working on

My growth plan is about clearer expectations, more manageable preparation and marking, and giving students feedback while they can still use it. Two targets are returning work within five business days and giving students practice before each summative assessment. One change I'd like to share is making more of what happens in class available afterward.

A whiteboard that stays

A couple of years ago, I learned the smartboard because preparing PowerPoints was taking me too long. I wanted something flexible. Now I use OneNote, with one page for each class in our class Notebook. What I write stays available to the students for the rest of the semester.

More than what I write

Knowing the page will still be there encourages me to add extra notes, reminders and screenshots. I can build an explanation as we go. I also feel less need to pause so everyone can photograph the board. The pauses can be for questions and comprehension.

The explanation stays too

I've also been recording my classes through Teams. The recordings live in a channel in our class Team, alongside access to the Notebook. Finding the videos is a bit clunky, but it's good enough for now. I'm not taking on the job of downloading and chaptering every recording.

A record for me

The saved transcripts let me check exam questions against how I actually taught the material. I've used that record to add theory questions based on class discussion. It should also help me build better lesson plans for future instructors, grounded in what actually happened in the classroom.

A fallback for students

Students can revisit an explanation or catch up when they can't attend and participate effectively. One student sent me this message about keeping up while working overnight shifts. That was a useful indication that the recordings were helping someone.

More confidence in what's available

Having the videos and whiteboards available gives me more confidence that students can access what we've covered. It encourages me to ask more of them. My lectures can be a source for assessment questions alongside the textbook and course notes. Access still leaves the question of what students actually learn from it.

Does that make class skippable?

That's a concern. Attendance isn't mandatory in my program, and recordings make opting out easier. But I've experienced excessive absenteeism while withholding information too. I'd rather make the information available and focus on giving my best to the students who show up. Ideally, students who are ill can stay home and catch up.

Here's where I get stuck

I can get caught up in making the explanation clear and the saved notes useful. Meanwhile, giving students room to grapple with the material is a goal I'm making less progress on. A walkthrough is something I can do live. A suitable independent exercise takes preparation I haven't consistently managed lately.

One example from this week

On October 26, we filled in this spreadsheet using textbook tables I'd collected into a PDF. There were a few conversions and extra calculations, but finding the right values was a big part of the exercise. With good written instructions, students could have tried it themselves. Instead, I filled it in on the projector.

The part I did for them

I suspect many students simply copied the numbers as I entered them. Looking up those values was one of the skills I wanted them to practise, and I'd done that part for them. The completed workbook is now viewable and downloadable from our OneNote page, so they can inspect it afterward. That still leaves the practice they missed in class.

Making room for practice

I've also given this class ten or fifteen minutes to try something and found they hadn't started. That's discouraging. In a computer lab, I sometimes feel like I'm on in the background. I could restrict the computers or prepare more try-first activities, but I can't fix everything this semester. I need to focus on a few things at a time.

What I'd like to hear from you

How do you balance demonstrations with time for students to work things out themselves? What has worked in your classes?
